claims.text: Corrosion protection in Q235 steel is governed by the formation of a dense, adherent oxide scale.
At 700–900 °C, aggressive-salt exposure accelerates oxidation kinetics relative to room-temperature exposure.
High-temperature exposure produces a more uniform and protective oxide film than room-temperature exposure.
Room-temperature exposure produces a relatively discontinuous and nonuniform oxide scale.
As-received Q235 steel has a native oxide film.
As-received Q235 steel has a typical ferritic microstructure.
The governing structural mediator is the continuity, density, and adherence of the surface oxide scale.
The surface oxide scale is predominantly magnetite.
Rapid diffusion and oxidation at high temperature promote formation of a coherent, dense, self-healing oxide layer.
The coherent, dense oxide layer acts as a barrier against further corrosive attack.
Slower, heterogeneous oxide growth at room temperature provides poorer corrosion protection.
High-temperature-exposed samples will have a lower net mass change than room-temperature-exposed samples.
High-temperature-exposed samples will form a thicker oxide scale than room-temperature-exposed samples.
High-temperature-exposed samples will form a more uniform oxide scale than room-temperature-exposed samples.
High-temperature-exposed samples will exhibit lower corrosion rates than room-temperature-exposed samples.
The proposed mechanism is limited to Q235 steel with a native oxide film under the defined salt and temperature conditions.
Changes in alloy composition or additional surface treatments may alter the corrosion behavior.

contradictions.description: High temperature is said to accelerate oxidation and produce a thicker oxide scale, while also producing a lower net mass change. These statements could be reconciled by distinguishing initial scale growth from subsequent corrosion or spallation, but that temporal or mass-balance distinction is not provided.
